items.title: 2 TV Shows Take on Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX
items.summary: The limited series “The Altruists” and the documentary “The Boy Who Stole Billions?” offer different takes on the crypto exchange founder’s role in one of the largest frauds in history.
items.full_text:
Title: 2 TV Shows Take on Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/27/business/media/sam-bankman-fried-ftx-altruists.html

Published Time: Fri, 27 Nov 2026 21:28:48 GMT

Markdown Content:
It was July 2023 and Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the collapsed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, needed a distraction.

Under house arrest at his parents’ home in Palo Alto, Calif., waiting to be tried for defrauding his customers of $8 billion, he spent his days readying his defense, watching South Korean noir on Netflix and playing video games. He was also talking to Nanette Burstein, an acclaimed documentary filmmaker.

As the two discussed what television shows Mr. Bankman-Fried should watch, Ms. Burstein suggested “The Dropout,” the Hulu mini-series starring Amanda Seyfried as the former Theranos chief executive Elizabeth Holmes, who is now serving an 11-year sentence for fraud.

He immediately batted away the recommendation.

“They’re just going to do a depiction of me, and it’s not going to be real,” Ms. Burstein remembers him saying. “So I can’t watch what’s been done on Elizabeth Holmes, because I just know that’s going to happen to me.”

Three years later, Mr. Bankman-Fried is getting the Elizabeth Holmes treatment. Currently serving a 25-year prison sentence, he is the focus of “[The Altruists](https://www.netflix.com/title/81681910),” an eight-episode scripted series that debuted on Nov. 19, and “[The Boy Who Stole Billions?](https://www.docnyc.net/film/the-boy-who-stole-billions/),” a three-part docuseries that will start streaming on Amazon on Monday.

The projects offer notably different takes. The fictionalized series, created by Graham Moore, paints Mr. Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison, his business partner and sometime girlfriend, as a neurodivergent, white-collar Bonnie and Clyde, whose dysfunctional relationship led to FTX’s downfall. The docuseries puts Mr. Bankman-Fried center stage and is skeptical that his punishment fits the crime.

Image

Mr. Bankman-Fried in “The Boy Who Stole Billions?,” an Amazon documentary that will start streaming on Monday.Credit...Amazon Prime

“The Boy Who Stole Billions?” is built around video interviews with Mr. Bankman-Fried from prison. Ms. Burstein argues that the 25-year sentence feels extreme, noting that everyone who lost money was repaid and that Mr. Bankman-Fried’s investments in other companies, like [Anthropic](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/technology/sam-bankman-fried-anthropic.html), were rich enough that they could have covered his losses.

“I really like Sam, and I think he did and does want to save the world,” said Ms. Burstein, whose previous subjects include Hillary Clinton (“Hillary”), Elizabeth Taylor (“Elizabeth Taylor: The Lost Tapes”) and Robert Evans (“The Kid Stays in the Picture”).

“I think that the way that he saw money being moved around was not necessarily the way that other people thought was OK to do,” she added. “I think it’s complicated because he had illiquid investments that were amazing. So in his mind, he’s like, ‘Well, what was the problem?’ And I understand why he thinks that.”

Mr. Bankman-Fried said he had participated in the project with the goal of clearing his name.

“I’m hoping that it tells at least some piece of the real story — which would still be more than most other media has,” he wrote in an email from the federal prison in Lompoc, Calif. He has yet to see the documentary.

Image

Mr. Bankman-Fried at the Crypto Bahamas conference in Nassau in 2022.Credit...Erika P. Rodriguez for The New York Times

Ms. Burstein also had access to his parents and to associates who were found to be co-conspirators and also served prison time.

[Ms. Ellison](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/07/20/technology/ftx-caroline-ellison-bankman-fried.html), the former chief executive of the cryptocurrency hedge fund Alameda Research, a sister company to FTX, declined to participate. (Ms. Ellison, a star witness for the prosecution at Mr. Bankman-Fried’s trial, was [sentenced to two years in prison](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/09/24/technology/caroline-ellison-ftx-sentence.html) for her role in the fraud; she was released in January, after 14 months.)

In “The Altruists,” Mr. Moore (who won an Oscar for his screenplay for “The Imitation Game”) frames his series as a complicated love story between two math geniuses. Their quest to make the world a better place by giving away most of their profits — as part of the [effective altruism](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/06/17/opinion/effective-altruism-philanthropy-charity.html) movement, a philosophy that focuses on using data to calculate how to do the most good for as many people as possible — was thwarted by excessive ambition and risk. Anthony Boyle (“House of Guinness”) plays Mr. Bankman-Fried while Julia Garner (“Inventing Anna”) portrays Ms. Ellison.

FTX failed, Mr. Moore believes, because Mr. Bankman-Fried and Ms. Ellison just couldn’t quit each other and key decisions, like removing guardrails on Alameda Research’s ability to trade, were made emotionally rather than rationally. Mr. Moore contends that the pair started out with the best of intentions and “ended up turning each other into people who did the exact opposite of the thing they set out to do.”

“I do not believe that what happened at FTX and Alameda would have happened without both Sam or Caroline,” added Mr. Moore, who relied on reporting from New York magazine while also developing his own sources inside the case. “I don’t think that he would be in jail right now if not for her, nor do I think she would have gone to jail if not for him.”

Image

Ms. Ellison was a star witness at the fraud trial of Mr. Bankman-Fried in 2023.Credit...Jeenah Moon for The New York Times

Ms. Ellison, through her lawyer, declined to comment.

Lee Reiners, a lecturing fellow at Duke University and an expert witness in a class-action lawsuit against FTX, watched the first two episodes of “The Altruists” and was struck by the fictionalized take on the two protagonists.

“She’s portrayed as some brainiac femme fatale who is the one who gave Sam his confidence and spurred him on to do all these things,” he said. “The evidentiary record was quite clear that he seemed fairly indifferent to her personally.”

This is not the first time a scripted adaptation and a documentary arrived around the same time. “The People v. O.J. Simpson: American Crime Story,” a 10-part series, was released in February 2016, just months before Ezra Edelman’s five-part documentary, “O.J.: Made in America.”

The scripted series focused on the circus of the trial, while the documentary took a longer view, situating Mr. Simpson’s biography in the broader context of race, celebrity and America’s criminal justice system.

Miranda Banks, a professor at Loyola Marymount University’s School of Film and Television, said that those two projects complemented each other and that the same might hold for the dueling depictions of Mr. Bankman-Fried, whose motives appear as mysterious as those of Ms. Holmes.

“These are two people who are inaccessible because of their neurodivergent perception of the world,” Ms. Banks said. “The law has declared them guilty, but is there a kernel of something that we’re not understanding here that makes us want to dig a little deeper?”

Barbara Fried, Mr. Bankman-Fried’s mother, who interacted with the makers of “The Altruists” after only the show finished production, said she was trying to find a silver lining in the newfound attention on her son.

“The worst thing that could happen for him is the world would forget about him,” said Ms. Fried, a lawyer and law professor at Stanford, who has been posting articles on her [Substack](https://barbarafried1110.substack.com/) laying out the case for her son’s innocence. “So, in that sense, this attention is good news. It might be the first moment in which the world might actually entertain the thought that the perceived narrative of him being the devil incarnate doesn’t make sense.”

“The Altruists” and “The Boy Who Stole Billions?” are also being released in the wake of “You Can See Everything,” the three-hour documentary about Ms. Holmes that has [triumphed at the box office](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/25/business/media/elizabeth-holmes-clayface-box-office.html) and generated debates about [the nature of documentaries](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/24/opinion/elizabeth-holmes-you-can-see-everything.html) and the [liberties taken in the fictionalization of real-life stories.](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/09/arts/you-can-see-everything-amanda-seyfried.html)

Image

Elizabeth Holmes, the former chief executive of Theranos, speaking with the filmmaker Nathan Fielder in “You Can See Everything.”Credit...A24

The filmmakers do not consider their projects to be in competition; instead, they believe each could promote interest in the other.

“It’ll be really interesting to see these two things and to see it in light of so many people having seen the Elizabeth Holmes documentary,” Ms. Burstein said. “I think there’s a lot of power in a scripted series. It’s also a big responsibility.”

Mr. Moore said he was likewise eager to see Ms. Burstein’s documentary.

“The purpose of a piece of dramatic art like ‘The Altruists’ is not to say this is the final word on Sam and Caroline,” he said. “It’s to say these are the first words about Sam and Caroline to be heard by an audience who might not have spent the last four years as obsessed with it as I have. If watching our series gets someone to watch Nanette’s documentary, that’s a job well done on my part.”

Sam Trabucco, the former co-chief executive of Alameda Research who left Alameda before it shut down, is interviewed in the documentary and played by Alex Lawther in “The Altruists.” He has seen both shows.
